questions.q: What does this lesson say threat modeling is, and when it should happen?
options: A structured, deliberate practice of asking how a system could be attacked or misused, done at design time rather than after the fact
A penetration test performed after a system has already shipped
A once-a-year compliance audit of an org's permission sets
A feature of Salesforce Shield that automatically generates a list of vulnerabilities
questions.explain: Threat modeling is a design-time, structured practice -- the point is to catch design flaws on a whiteboard, before they're built, when fixing them is far cheaper than after an incident reveals them.

questions.q: In the STRIDE framework, which category does the question "could someone perform an action and later credibly deny having done it, because there's no reliable record?" belong to?
options: Spoofing
Repudiation
Denial of service
Elevation of privilege
questions.explain: Repudiation is specifically about whether an action can be credibly denied later due to a lack of reliable record -- a different concern from spoofing (pretending to be someone else) or denial of service (making the system unavailable).

questions.q: In the inbound integration example, what specific risk does the "Elevation of privilege" STRIDE question raise?
options: Whether the integration user's permission set allows editing only the Order fields it's supposed to touch
Whether the integration could exhaust the org's API call limits
Whether a leaked connected app secret or named credential could grant access beyond just Order data, up to broader admin-level actions
Whether the OAuth flow can be spoofed by a system other than the real order-management system
questions.explain: Elevation of privilege asks what the blast radius is if a credential leaks -- specifically whether it opens a path to more access than the integration was originally scoped for, distinct from tampering, denial of service, or spoofing concerns.

questions.q: Why does this lesson argue that going through all six STRIDE categories deliberately is more valuable than stopping at the most obvious threat?
options: Because Salesforce requires documentation of all six categories before Shield can be enabled
Because only the first three letters of STRIDE are actually relevant to Salesforce integrations
Because STRIDE guarantees that every possible threat will be found if all six letters are checked
Because different categories point at different controls, so a design that's airtight against one category (e.g., information disclosure) can still have a wide-open gap in another (e.g., repudiation)
questions.explain: The value of the full six-category pass is that it surfaces threats across different control domains -- stopping early risks missing a threat in a category nobody happened to think of unprompted.

questions.q: What does this lesson say about treating likelihood and impact as the same axis when prioritizing identified threats?
options: Likelihood and impact are two different axes; a low-likelihood, high-impact threat still deserves serious design attention, while a high-likelihood, low-impact one might only need a minor fix like a validation rule
They are the same axis, so a single severity rating is sufficient
Only impact matters -- likelihood should be ignored entirely when designing controls
Only likelihood matters -- a threat with low impact is not worth tracking regardless of how likely it is
questions.explain: The lesson distinguishes likelihood (how plausible) from impact (how severe) and warns against two opposite mistakes: treating every threat as equally urgent, and dismissing low-likelihood/high-impact threats as not worth addressing.
